stat-u2-t2-005: Experimental units are what the treatments are applied to.
The formulas are the treatments and the ratings are the response; the 40 volunteers receive the treatments.
stat-u2-t2-006: The response variable is what is measured after the treatment.
Which formula a subject uses is the treatment, not the response.
stat-u2-t2-007: A control group gets no treatment, a placebo, or the standard treatment.
Comparing with it shows how much of the change is due to the treatment.
stat-u2-t2-008: Random assignment decides which subjects get which treatment by chance.
It balances other variables across groups; random selection, not assignment, makes a sample represent a population.
stat-u2-t2-009: Responses vary from unit to unit even under the same treatment.
Using many units per treatment lets a real effect stand out from that chance variation.
stat-u2-t2-010: Some subjects improve just because they believe they are being treated.
Giving the control group a placebo lets that effect occur in both groups, so the comparison isolates the drug.
stat-u2-t2-011: Blinding keeps people from knowing which treatment a subject received.
Double-blind means both the subjects and those who interact with them or measure the response are unaware.
stat-u2-t2-012: Each review method was used with only one class.
The classes differ in time of day and students, so those differences are mixed up with the method.
stat-u2-t2-015: Gender is expected to affect the response, so group subjects by gender first.
Randomly assign the formulas within each gender; assigning by gender would confound gender with formula.
stat-u2-t2-016: Units in a block are similar with respect to a variable that affects the response.
Comparing treatments within each block removes that variable’s effect from the comparison.
stat-u2-t2-017: Each volunteer gets both formulas, one on each half of the head.
The two halves form a pair, and the side is randomized: a matched pairs design.
stat-u2-t2-018: A completely randomized design assigns all units to treatments by chance.
Arrival order or personal choice is not random assignment.
stat-u2-t2-019: Check two things: random selection (generalize) and random assignment (cause and effect).
This study has both, so causal conclusions apply to adults in the city.
stat-u2-t2-020: Random assignment is present, so cause and effect is supported.
The volunteers came from one gym, not a random sample, so generalize only to people like them.
stat-u2-t2-021: Ask whether chance alone (the random assignment) could plausibly produce a difference this large.
If not, the result is statistically significant; that is not the same as practically important.
stat-u2-s01-cp2-x01: The sample is the group data are actually collected from.
The 48,000 voters are the population; the 600 surveyed are the sample.
stat-u2-s01-cp2-x02: The population is the whole group the company wants to learn about.
That is today’s 12,000 boxes; the 40 weighed boxes are the sample.
stat-u2-s01-cp2-x03: A census measures every individual in the population.
420 households is small enough to reach, so there is no sampling variability (though errors can still occur).
stat-u2-s01-cp2-x04: Ask whether 38% describes the 250 students surveyed or the whole school.
It describes the sample, so it is a statistic.
stat-u2-s01-cp2-x05: “All U.S. households” is a whole population.
A number describing a population is a parameter.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x01: To measure a bulb’s lifetime, it must burn until it fails.
Testing every bulb would destroy the whole production run.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x02: Parameters describe populations (μ, σ, p); statistics describe samples (x̄, s, p̂).
A statistic estimates the matching parameter, so x̄ estimates μ.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x03: Before choosing a sample, you need a list of individuals to choose from.
That list is the sampling frame.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x04: Inference goes from what we see in a sample to what is true of a population.
Describing only the sample is not inference.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x05: 27.4 minutes was computed from 400 sampled workers.
So it is a statistic estimating the unknown population mean; individual commutes vary.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x06: A census of a huge population is hard to carry out carefully.
Many people are missed or answer badly; a careful sample can avoid those errors.
stat-u2-s01-cp1-x08: A statistic is computed from a sample; a parameter describes a whole population.
80 seniors and 1,000 voters are samples; all NBA players and all U.S. adults are populations.
stat-u2-s01-honors-x01: Compare the sampling frame with the population.
Card holders who did not borrow a book last year can never be chosen.
stat-u2-s01-honors-x02: Results generalize to the population that was randomly sampled.
That is Ohio high school students, not Ohio adults or all U.S. teens.
stat-u2-s01-honors-x03: A useful population definition says who, where and when.
Only the last choice names all three precisely.
stat-u2-s01-honors-x04: The sample came from online customers only.
In-store-only customers could not be selected, so the results may not apply to them.
stat-u2-s01-honors-x05: The margin of error comes from the formula for a random sample.
It covers only sampling variability, not bias from wording, undercoverage or nonresponse.
stat-u2-s01-honors-x06: A “representative” sample chosen by judgment can carry the chooser’s biases.
Random selection avoids that and lets probability describe how estimates vary.
stat-u2-s02-cp2-x01: Identical, well-mixed slips give every student the same chance.
Every group of 5 is equally likely, with no strata or clusters: an SRS.
stat-u2-s02-cp2-x02: Ask how the customers were chosen.
Taking whoever comes in first uses no chance at all: a convenience sample.
stat-u2-s02-cp2-x03: Students are divided into groups by grade.
Sampling randomly from every group makes the grades strata.
stat-u2-s02-cp2-x04: The flights are chosen at random, then every passenger on them is surveyed.
Selecting whole groups is cluster sampling.
stat-u2-s02-cp2-x05: The inspector starts at a random item among the first 20.
Then every 20th item is taken: a systematic random sample.
stat-u2-s02-cp2-x06: A random number generator gives numbers, not people.
Labels connect each number to one individual, so chance does the choosing.
stat-u2-s02-cp1-x03: Incomes are similar within neighborhoods and differ between them.
That makes neighborhoods ideal strata; sampling only two neighborhoods would miss most of the variation.
stat-u2-s02-cp1-x04: The residents are spread over 50 towns and travel is expensive.
Choosing a few towns at random and interviewing there saves travel.
stat-u2-s02-cp1-x05: In a systematic sample, the random start fixes the whole sample.
So two neighbors on the list can never be chosen together; an SRS allows every group.
stat-u2-s02-honors-x01: Stratification helps only when the strata differ in the response.
Study time likely varies by grade; it is unrelated to the first letter of a last name.
stat-u2-s02-honors-x02: Look at the steps: districts, then schools, then classrooms, each chosen at random.
Sampling in several stages is a multistage sample.
stat-u2-s02-honors-x03: People in the same building tend to be alike (mostly renters or mostly owners).
So each building adds little new information compared with the same number of residents chosen separately.
stat-u2-s03-cp2-x01: The listeners decide whether to call.
People who choose to respond usually feel strongly, so the sample is biased.
stat-u2-s03-cp2-x02: The sampling frame is a list of landlines.
Adults with only cell phones cannot be selected.
stat-u2-s03-cp2-x03: The 800 were chosen at random, but only 210 answered.
If nonresponders differ from responders, the results are biased.
stat-u2-s03-cp2-x04: Look for words that push toward one answer.
“Hard-working” and “deserve” lead respondents to say yes.
stat-u2-s03-cp2-x05: The coach is an authority figure asking about breaking a rule.
Students are likely to say no, so skipping is under-reported.
stat-u2-s03-cp2-x06: Bias comes from how people are chosen, not how many.
More volunteers or easier-to-reach people keep the same bias; random selection from a full list removes it.
stat-u2-s03-cp1-x01: The sampling frame is property tax records, which list homeowners.
Renters and people without homes are not on that list.
stat-u2-s03-cp1-x02: The question opens with a reason to say yes.
That leads respondents, so the yes percent is likely higher than with neutral wording.
stat-u2-s03-cp1-x04: Bias is a systematic error in the method; variability is chance error.
More data from the same method shrinks variability but keeps the bias.
stat-u2-s03-honors-x03: Undercoverage means some people cannot be reached at all.
Adding cell numbers lets cell-only adults be selected; prizes or more landline calls do not.
stat-u2-s03-honors-x04: Viewers chose whether to text in, so that sample is voluntary response.
A large biased sample is still biased; the random sample is more trustworthy.
stat-u2-s04-cp2-x01: Ask whether the researchers assigned the diets.
They only recorded what people ate: observational.
stat-u2-s04-cp2-x02: Ask whether the teacher assigned the treatments.
She randomly assigned flashcards or the game: an experiment.
stat-u2-s04-cp2-x03: Look for who decides the treatment.
In an experiment, the researcher does; in an observational study, the researcher just watches.
stat-u2-s04-cp2-x04: The students chose whether to play an instrument; nothing was assigned.
So other differences could explain the scores; only an association is shown.
stat-u2-s04-cp2-x05: Random assignment spreads other variables evenly across the groups.
Then the treatment is the only systematic difference, so it can explain the response.
stat-u2-s04-cp2-x06: The researcher changes nothing and only measures.
So it is an observational study.
stat-u2-s04-cp1-x01: An experiment would require assigning some women to smoke.
Smoking is harmful, so that would be unethical.
stat-u2-s04-cp1-x02: A lurking variable is related to both taking supplements and getting colds.
Healthier habits fit: they go with taking supplements and with fewer colds.
stat-u2-s04-cp1-x03: No treatment is assigned, so it is observational.
Subjects are followed forward in time, so it is prospective.
stat-u2-s04-cp1-x04: No treatment was assigned by the researchers.
They look back at existing records, so it is retrospective.
stat-u2-s04-honors-x01: People choose standing desks themselves, so other differences may explain less back pain.
Only random assignment removes that; more observational data cannot.
stat-u2-s04-honors-x02: Ask which treatments could ethically and practically be assigned.
Children cannot be assigned to live near a highway; the others can be experiments.
stat-u2-s04-honors-x03: Comparing within income groups removes only income as an explanation.
Diet, exercise or health awareness could still differ between buyers and nonbuyers.
stat-u2-s05-cp2-x01: Ask what the researcher deliberately applies to each experimental unit.
Responses are measured afterward; lurking variables are not imposed.
stat-u2-s05-cp2-x02: The response variable is the outcome measured after the treatment.
Music or silence is the treatment; the test score is measured.
stat-u2-s05-cp2-x03: Studying in silence is the usual condition.
It gives a baseline to compare with music.
stat-u2-s05-cp2-x04: Students who choose music may differ in other ways, such as study habits.
Random assignment balances those differences across the groups.
stat-u2-s05-cp1-x01: Factors are the explanatory variables the researcher controls.
Dose and time of day are factors; their 3 × 2 = 6 combinations are the treatments.
stat-u2-s05-cp1-x02: Individual batteries of the same brand vary.
With one battery per brand, that variation could explain the difference.
stat-u2-s05-cp1-x05: Recall the four principles: comparison, random assignment, control, replication.
Letting subjects choose and using one unit per treatment break those principles.
stat-u2-s05-honors-x01: Diet A always goes with the warm room and Diet B with the cool room.
So any difference could come from temperature instead of diet.
stat-u2-s05-honors-x02: Similar units respond more alike, so there is less noise.
But conclusions then apply only to units like those.
stat-u2-s05-honors-x03: Over time, people can change for many reasons, such as natural recovery or the placebo effect.
A comparison group experiences those too, so the difference isolates the treatment.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x01: A placebo looks like the real treatment.
It has no active ingredient, so it measures the effect of just being treated.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x02: The placebo effect is a response to receiving a treatment, not to its ingredient.
Belief alone can change outcomes such as pain or mood.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x03: Blinding keeps someone from knowing the treatment.
Single-blind: one group (subjects or evaluators) does not know; double-blind: neither does.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x04: Double-blind refers to two groups of people being unaware.
Neither the subjects nor those measuring the response know the treatment.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x05: Confounding happens when two variables change together.
Then their effects on the response cannot be separated.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x06: Each warm-up was used with only one team.
Varsity and JV players differ in age, fitness and experience, so team level is mixed with the warm-up.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x07: Subjects can be blinded only if they cannot tell which treatment they got.
Identical bottles and identical-looking pills work; surgery and different sports cannot be hidden.
stat-u2-s06-cp2-x09: Each method was used with only one class at one time of day.
Class and time differences are mixed with the method, so the game’s effect cannot be isolated.
stat-u2-s06-cp1-x01: The placebo group shows how many get relief without the drug: 41%.
The medicine’s effect is the difference, about 64% − 41% = 23 points.
stat-u2-s06-cp1-x02: Each program is always taught at one time of day.
So the effect of the program cannot be separated from the effect of time of day.
stat-u2-s06-cp1-x03: Blinding needs treatments that feel the same to subjects.
Patients know whether they had surgery, though the evaluators can still be blinded.
stat-u2-s06-cp1-x04: The teachers scoring the test know which students used the program.
Their expectations could raise or lower scores, so the evaluators should be blinded.
stat-u2-s06-cp1-x06: Double-blind: subjects and evaluators do not know the treatment.
A placebo has no active ingredient, and random assignment is still required.
stat-u2-s06-honors-x01: The diet group got two things: the diet and weekly coaching.
The control group got neither, so coaching is confounded with the diet.
stat-u2-s06-honors-x02: The drug’s effect is the difference between the groups, not each group’s improvement.
No difference means no evidence that the drug adds anything beyond placebo or natural recovery.
stat-u2-s06-honors-x03: Expectations change behavior: stress, diet and taking medication as directed.
Evaluators who know the treatment can also read measurements differently.
stat-u2-s07-cp2-x01: In a completely randomized design, chance alone assigns treatments.
No blocks or pairs are formed first, and units do not choose.
stat-u2-s07-cp2-x02: A block groups similar units before treatments are assigned.
The units are alike in a way that is expected to affect the response.
stat-u2-s07-cp2-x03: Twins form natural pairs of very similar units.
A coin flip assigns the methods within each pair: matched pairs.
stat-u2-s07-cp2-x04: Blocking is used for a variable that affects the response.
Comparing programs within each gender removes gender differences from the comparison.
stat-u2-s07-cp2-x05: Each student uses both pens, so each student is his or her own pair.
A coin flip sets the order: a matched pairs design.
